newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila shares tumble, seen reeling further.
newsitem.headline: Manila shares tumble, seen reeling further.

text.p: Philippine shares slumped on Monday to their lowest levels since the devaluation of the peso more than a month ago and analysts expect no let-up in the sell-off in coming days.

Traders said the U.S. Dow Jones index's 247-point fall last Friday, the second-biggest single-day drop in its history, weighed down Philippine shares, aided by the peso hitting a record low 30 to the dollar in early morning trade.
The main index shed 80.26 points, or 3.28 percent, to close at a 21-month low of 2,368.67 points.
"We may see more bloodbaths during the week. The Dow is weak and stocks forever hinge on the peso," said Helen Alvarez, research director at All Asia Securities.

"The market took a big hit today but it will go down further. People are just now realising that second-half growth may be lower, and until they accept the situation there won't be any rally," said Norman Villamin, research head at UBS Securities (East Asia) Ltd.
Brokers expect the market to test the support level of 2,200 points in the next few days labelling any runup as merely technical in nature.

"We are looking at the support of 2,200 and hopefully not lower otherwise we may give 'Philippines 2000' a new meaning," one foreign broker said, referring to a Ramos administration programme to make the country a newly industrialised state by the end of the century.
Jonathan Ravelas, head of sales at Asian Capital Equities, expects the U.S. Federal Reserve's Open Market Committee interest rate policy meeting on Tuesday to also keep some investors nervous.
For the rest of the year, analysts foresaw a lacklustre equities market.
The main index has shed 1,078.93 points, or 44.05 percent, since its all-time high of 3,447.60 points in February.
It has so far lost 332.47 points, or 12.30 percent, from its close of 2,701.14 on July 11 when the peso was allowed to float in a wider band, effectively devaluing the currency.

"Foreign investors are moving out of Southeast Asia to Eastern Europe or Latin America. If third-quarter results and first-half gross national product (GNP) are better than expected and if the comprehensive tax bill is passed, we may see some gains but then again, they do not guarantee a major reversal," said Raul Ruiz, vice-president at Sun Hung Kai Securities Phils.
Alvarez adds that if the peso falls below 30 to the dollar, company earnings forecasts may have to be downgraded.
Anscor-Hagedorn Securities vice-president Noel Reyes expects share prices to suffer for the rest of the year from the effects of the peso's depreciation.

All-Asia's Alvarez adds: "The market will be indeterminate for the rest of the year. It has to convince players of its upside but with volatilities there are also opportunities. We tell investors this: Do not expect any bulls but do not expect a bust either."
